candidates.attacker_control: Untrusted HTML passed to the public API. AntiSamy.scan(String) defaults to scanType SAX (AntiSamy.java lines 72-79, 96-103), so an attacker's markup flows through the NekoHTML SAX parser into MagicSAXFilter.startElement/endElement. The attacker fully controls the element name ("style"), its attributes (names and values) and its text content.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The tag itself is still restricted by the policy (style must exist with action validate in the active policy); the emitted attributes are quoted/escaped by the serializer, so this is not a generic string-injection; the CSS content remains separately sanitized; all bundled policies set useXHTML=true; browsers commonly do not fire load/error on <style>, so the strongest script-execution path is conditional; the DOM scanner (AntiSamyDOMScanner.actionValidate lines 359-371 followed by processAttributes) does apply the attribute whitelist, so the defect is path-specific, not global; MagicSAXFilter also uses the reversed test "style".endsWith(element.localpart), which only broadens the special case to tags named e/le/yle/tyle and is not itself exploitable with the bundled policies.
candidates.impact: Attribute-level sanitizer bypass in the default (SAX) scan path: attributes that the policy is supposed to strip or validate are preserved verbatim on <style> elements in the "cleaned" output, including inline event handlers, the style attribute, and any other global/unknown attribute (also bypassing onInvalid=removeAttribute/removeTag/filterTag semantics). If the sanitized fragment is re-parsed by a browser/HTML consumer that fires such handlers on <style> or otherwise acts on the injected attribute (e.g. CSS-based UI redress/overlay, or legacy browsers where style-element handlers/schemes execute), this becomes script execution in the victim's origin; more generally it defeats the library's documented whitelist guarantee for that element.
candidates.prerequisites: Application calls AntiSamy.scan(...) through the SAX path (the default) and uses a policy in which the style tag has action="validate" (the bundled default antisamy.xml does: <tag name="style" action="validate"> at src/main/resources/antisamy.xml:806). Realizing script execution from the smuggled attributes additionally depends on the consuming browser/context (e.g. whether it honors the smuggled event handler/scheme on a style element, or on an unvalidated style attribute value), so the guaranteed effect is the whitelist bypass itself.
candidates.root_cause: In MagicSAXFilter.startElement, when a validated tag is the style element (isStyle), the code pushes Ops.CSS, records the CSS content buffer and stores the parser's original XMLAttributes object (cssAttributes = attributes) without running the per-attribute validation/whitelist loop that every other validated element goes through. At endElement (Ops.CSS branch), when the sanitized CSS is non-empty, the element is re-emitted with those stored, unvalidated attributes (super.startElement(element, cssAttributes, ...)). Consequently attribute-level policy rules (allowed attribute list, allowed value literals/regexes, onInvalid actions such as removeAttribute/removeTag/filterTag) are not enforced for <style> elements in the SAX path, whereas the DOM scanner validates them (actionValidate -> processStyleTag, then processAttributes). Additionally, the same block also treats the style *attribute* specially before the policy check, so a style attribute is CSS-scanned and kept even when the policy does not allow it on the element.
candidates.title: SAX scanner (<style> handling) emits unvalidated attributes, bypassing the policy attribute whitelist
candidates.trace: Input e.g. <style onload="alert(1)">body{color:red}</style> (or an unvalidated style/title/id/etc. attribute). NekoHTML fires startElement for the style tag -> policy.getTagByLowercaseName("style") returns a validate tag -> the validate branch computes isStyle and stores cssAttributes = attributes, skipping the attribute loop at lines 283-351 entirely -> endElement sees Ops.CSS, CSS-scans the content, and because the cleaned CSS is non-empty calls super.startElement(element, cssAttributes, ...) with the original attributes, then characters/endElement -> the serializer writes the <style> start tag including every attacker-supplied attribute. The DOM path for the same input removes attributes not in the policy (processAttributes), proving the whitelist is intended to apply to style tags.
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no exploit was attempted. Browser-side execution of smuggled attributes on a <style> element (and of an unvalidated style attribute) was not runtime-verified, and the serializer/parser library behavior (NekoHTML XMLAttributes lifetime, Xerces/Xalan output escaping) was reasoned from source, not observed. The exact upstream fix commit/CVE mapping for this snapshot could not be confirmed offline.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper/incomplete input validation leading to XSS / policy bypass (CWE-79, CWE-20, CWE-693)

coverage_summary: Coverage: source scope reports 126 files at the source root / 125 model-visible files (1 file excluded by sensitive-name-or-path filter; 0 excluded for size/symlinks/binary). I inspected all 27 main Java files (org.owasp.validator.html, .css, .scan, .model, .util) and all 6 test Java files, plus pom.xml, README, and the policy resources (antisamy.xml read in detail across directives, common regexps/attributes, tag rules, CSS rules; the other five antisamy-*.xml files checked by targeted searches for directives/useXHTML/embedStyleSheets). The very large third-party test resources under src/test/resources/s/ (minified JS/CSS/HTML used by the performance test) were not reviewed line-by-line. The P1 relation index is explicitly partial (33 parsed Java files, 312 omitted files, 505 symbols, 1043 unresolved calls, no control-flow/data-flow, annotations as name candidates only); edges were used only for navigation (e.g. confirming the ExternalCssScanner override has no incoming call edge) and every candidate was re-checked against source text.
limitations: No execution, tests, scanners or exploit payloads were run; all conclusions are source-level.
Runtime behavior of third-party components (NekoHTML parser, Batik CSS parser, Xalan transformer, Xerces serializers) was reasoned from their usage, not verified.
The relation index provides syntax-level navigation only; it does not prove reachability, data flow or exploitability, and cannot confirm or refute the candidate.
The exact upstream fix/CVE identity for this snapshot (intended by the VUL4J case) could not be confirmed without external references, so the candidate is a lead, not a confirmed vulnerability.
The condition for browser execution of smuggled <style> attributes (and of an unvalidated style attribute) is environment-dependent and was not runtime-verified.

rejected_leads.lead: AntiSamyDOMScanner.processStyleTag sanitizes only ele.getFirstChild() of a <style> element, leaving sibling text/CDATA nodes (converted by stripCData) untouched inside the raw-text style element, which could allow CSS/HTML breakout in non-XHTML output.
rejected_leads.reason: Source shows the first-child-only scan (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java 391-468) and that non-element siblings are passed through, but I could not establish from source that the NekoHTML DOMFragmentParser ever produces more than one child node for style content (the CssScanner CDATA regex and strip-cdata-delims=false handling suggest a single text node), and all bundled policies set useXHTML=true so such content is output-escaped. Not enough evidence for a concrete exploit path.

rejected_leads.lead: stripNonValidXMLCharacters uses invalidXmlCharsMatcher.matches() before replaceAll(), so invalid XML characters are stripped only when the whole input consists of invalid characters.
rejected_leads.reason: The logic bug is real (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java 786-793), but the security consequence (parser differential/DoS in NekoHTML) cannot be established from this repository's source; the observable effect is that control characters remain in the parsed input rather than a demonstrated sanitizer bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: ExternalCssScanner.parseImportedStylesheets is never invoked because its parameter type ArrayList does not override the base method's List<String> signature (CssScanner.java 229-232 vs ExternalCssScanner.java 73-74), silently disabling the embedStyleSheets feature.
rejected_leads.reason: Verified as dead code (the relation index also shows no incoming call edge to the ExternalCssScanner method), but the impact is a non-functional feature, i.e. imported stylesheets are ignored, which is more restrictive, not less. If the override did run, the SSRF risk of fetching attacker-chosen @import URLs would be the security concern, but embedStyleSheets=false in every bundled policy and the code is unreachable in this snapshot, so no exploitable impact.

rejected_leads.lead: AntiSamyDOMScanner.removePI calls removeNode(node) and then node.getParentNode().removeChild(node), which dereferences a now-null parent (potential unhandled NullPointerException / DoS on processing instructions).
rejected_leads.reason: The NPE-looking sequence is visible (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java 686-690), but whether NekoHTML's DOMFragmentParser produces ProcessingInstruction nodes for attacker input is unverified, and the effect would be an exception (availability) rather than a sanitizer bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: CssValidator.lexicalValueToString returns raw SAC_STRING_VALUE/SAC_IDENT/SAC_URI text (quotes only added when a space is present), and CssHandler.property concatenates these unescaped values into the cleaned CSS.
rejected_leads.reason: Every value is validated against the property's literals/regexes with Pattern.matches() on the lowercased string first; with the bundled policies the reachable character set for CSS values excludes '<', '>' and ';', and string values are written into attribute contexts that are quote-escaped by the serializer. No concrete injection could be demonstrated from the resource policies.

rejected_leads.lead: SSRF via @import handling in ExternalCssScanner (HttpClient fetch of attacker-chosen offsiteURL/onsiteURL, URIUtils/normalize checks).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires the non-default directive embedStyleSheets=true (false in all bundled policies), and the fetching method is currently unreachable because of the signature mismatch noted above.

summary: AntiSamy 1.5.5-SNAPSHOT (owasp/antisamy) source review. I read all 27 main Java files (HTML scanner, SAX filter, DOM scanner, CSS scanner/handler/validator, policy model/parser, serializers, URI/XML utils), the 6 test classes, pom.xml/README, and the bundled policy XML (antisamy.xml in detail; other policies via targeted search). One source-verified defect stands out: in the SAX scanner (the default scan path, AntiSamy.scan(String) -> AntiSamy.SAX), attributes of <style> elements are never run through the policy attribute whitelist; the original parser attribute set is stashed at startElement and re-emitted verbatim at endElement. The DOM scanner does validate them, so the SAX path is an inconsistent bypass of the policy model. I submit that as the single candidate. Other suspicious areas (DOM firstChild-only CSS scan, matches()-vs-find() in stripNonValidXMLCharacters, dead ExternalCssScanner override, removePI NPE, CSS value reconstruction) are listed as rejected/unconfirmed leads because their security impact could not be established from source alone.
